question: The Eiffel Tower, built from wrought iron, is measurably taller in July than in January, by roughly the length of a pencil. Why?
alternative_answers: The metal expands when it is hot
Summer temperatures make the structure expand
Metal contracts in the cold and expands in warmth
source_excerpt: the top of the tower may shift away from the sun by up to 18 cm (7 in) due to thermal expansion of the metal

extra.verification_notes: Thermal expansion of the wrought-iron structure makes the tower taller in summer, commonly cited as about 15 cm; no newer developments contradict this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower).

explanation: Metals expand when heated and contract when cooled. The tower is made of about 7,300 tonnes of wrought iron, and over roughly 300 metres of height the tiny expansion of every beam adds up. On hot summer days the structure grows by up to about 15 centimetres and shrinks again in winter. The sun also warms one side more than the other, so the top of the tower leans slightly away from the sun during the day.

question: From 1889 the Eiffel Tower was the tallest man-made structure on Earth. In which city was the skyscraper that finally overtook it in 1930?
source_excerpt: In 1930, the tower lost the title of the world's tallest structure when the Chrysler Building in New York City was completed.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the Eiffel Tower is tall but rarely realise it held the world record for four decades; the dethroning city is deducible from the 1930 skyscraper boom.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Eiffel Tower article confirms the Chrysler Building in New York City overtook the Eiffel Tower in 1930, and a historical fact like this can't be made stale by later events.

explanation: The Chrysler Building took the record in 1930, only to lose it to the Empire State Building a year later.

question: Two 88-storey twin towers linked by a double-decker skybridge were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004. Which capital city are they in?
source_excerpt: a double decker skybridge connecting the two towers on the 41st and 42nd floors

extra.why_interesting: Many players picture the twin towers but place them in the wrong Asian city; the skybridge detail is the foothold that identifies them.
extra.verification_notes: Petronas Towers (88 storeys, double-decker skybridge, tallest 1998–2004) are in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia's capital, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petronas_Towers

explanation: The Petronas Towers' skybridge isn't bolted to either tower; it sits on sliding bearings so the two towers can sway independently in the wind.

question: The Golden Gate Bridge is painted a reddish orange and contains no gold at all. What does the 'Golden Gate' in its name actually refer to?
alternative_answers: The entrance to San Francisco Bay
source_excerpt: the Golden Gate, the one-mile-wide (1.6 km) strait connecting San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean

extra.why_interesting: Nearly everyone assumes the name describes the bridge itself, and is puzzled by its orange colour; the answer reveals the name predates the bridge entirely.
extra.verification_notes: The bridge is named after the Golden Gate strait it spans, and it is painted international orange with no gold, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Explorer John C. Fremont named the entrance to San Francisco Bay the Golden Gate in 1846, nearly a century before the bridge opened in 1937.

question: In 1968 the City of London sold its 19th-century London Bridge to an American businessman, who shipped it across the Atlantic and rebuilt it stone by stone. In which US state does it stand today?
source_excerpt: The Arizona bridge is a reinforced concrete structure clad in the original masonry of the 1830s bridge.

extra.why_interesting: A London landmark standing in the American desert is delightful in itself; the player who knows the story gets a payoff, and others can take a sporting guess at a US state.
extra.verification_notes: The 1830s London Bridge was sold in 1968 to Robert McCulloch and stands in Lake Havasu City, Arizona; the article mentions no relocation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Bridge_(Lake_Havasu_City)).

explanation: Robert McCulloch rebuilt it over a man-made channel at Lake Havasu City in the Arizona desert, where it reopened in 1971.

question: The architect of the Sydney Opera House quit the project in 1966 after a bitter row with the government and never returned to see his building finished. Which European country was he from?
source_excerpt: he had never returned to Australia to see the completed opera house.

extra.why_interesting: Australia's most famous building was designed by a foreigner who never saw it finished; players assume an Australian architect, and the sailing-boat forms hint at a seafaring Nordic nation.
extra.verification_notes: Utzon, a Dane, resigned in 1966 and never returned to Australia to see the finished Opera House; no later event changes this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B8rn_Utzon).

explanation: Jorn Utzon never saw the Opera House in person after leaving, though he was later reconciled with it and received architecture's Pritzker Prize in 2003.

question: Engineers feared the Hoover Dam's enormous concrete mass would take more than a century to cool down and would crack as it did. To speed it up, they embedded hundreds of kilometres of pipes carrying what?
source_excerpt: Cool river water would be poured through the pipes, followed by ice-cold water from a refrigeration plant

extra.why_interesting: Players expect concrete just sits and hardens; learning that it generates enough heat to need an industrial fridge for a century is the surprise, and the answer is deducible once the stem frames it as a cooling problem.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms 125-year cooling estimate and 937 km of embedded pipes carrying river water then ice-cold refrigerated water, so 'chilled water' is acceptable.

explanation: Over 900 kilometres of steel pipe ran through the blocks, fed by an on-site refrigeration plant, and once the concrete had cooled the pipes were filled with grout.

question: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest man-made structure on Earth from its completion until a European cathedral spire finally overtook it. Roughly how long did it hold that record?
source_excerpt: the Great Pyramid was the world's tallest human-made structure for more than 3,700 years.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the pyramids are old but underestimate how long humanity failed to build anything taller; the span runs from the Bronze Age to the Middle Ages.
extra.verification_notes: The Great Pyramid held the tallest-structure record for roughly 3,700–3,900 years until a medieval cathedral spire overtook it, so 'About 4,000 years' is the closest option (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza).

explanation: Finished around 2560 BC, it was only passed by Lincoln Cathedral's spire in about 1311, a reign of roughly 3,800 years.

question: In which year did the Channel Tunnel open to traffic between England and France?
source_excerpt: formally inaugurated on 6 May 1994 by French President François Mitterrand and Queen Elizabeth II at a ceremony in Calais

extra.why_interesting: Players tend to place the tunnel either in the Thatcher era or around the millennium; pinning the decade needs real recall.
extra.verification_notes: Channel Tunnel was officially opened 6 May 1994 and began freight and passenger services in 1994, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_Tunnel).

explanation: Queen Elizabeth II and President Mitterrand opened it in May 1994, and its 38-kilometre undersea stretch is still the longest of any tunnel in the world.

question: Built around 126 AD, which Roman building still holds the record for the world's largest dome made of unreinforced concrete?
source_excerpt: Almost two thousand years after it was built, the Pantheon's dome is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume concrete records belong to modern engineering; a Roman building holding one nearly two thousand years later is the surprise, and 'Roman dome' narrows it to one famous candidate.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Pantheon (c. 126 AD, Hadrian) still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome; I did not search for newer challengers.

explanation: Its 43-metre dome gets lighter towards the top, with pumice mixed into the concrete, and is crowned by an open hole that lets rain fall straight onto the floor.

question: Opened in 1994, which tunnel holds the record for the longest stretch of any tunnel running beneath the sea, about 38 kilometres of it?
source_excerpt: the longest underwater section of any tunnel in the world, at 37.9 km (23.5 miles)

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the record for undersea tunnelling belongs to Japan or to some newer mega-project; the 1994 date and the sea clue steer them to a tunnel they already know, which turns out to hold the record outright.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Channel Tunnel opened in 1994 and has the world's longest undersea section at 37.9 km, with no newer tunnel exceeding it.

explanation: Japan's Seikan Tunnel is longer overall, but the Channel Tunnel has the longest undersea section ever built, roughly 38 kilometres between Folkestone and Coquelles.

question: The copper skin of the Statue of Liberty hangs on an iron skeleton designed by an engineer whose own most famous work rose in Paris a few years later. What is that work?
source_excerpt: Eiffel and his structural engineer, Maurice Koechlin, decided to abandon the pier and instead build an iron truss tower.

extra.why_interesting: Players file the Statue of Liberty under America and the Eiffel Tower under France as unrelated icons; the stem's clues (iron skeleton, Paris, a few years later) let them deduce that the same engineer stands behind both.
extra.verification_notes: Eiffel designed the Statue of Liberty's iron skeleton (1886) and his most famous work, the Eiffel Tower, opened in Paris in 1889; no newer event affects this.

explanation: Gustave Eiffel designed the statue's internal iron framework in the early 1880s, then built his tower for the 1889 Paris World's Fair.

question: For some 3,800 years the Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest structure on Earth. What kind of building finally overtook it in medieval England around the year 1300?
source_excerpt: Tallest in the world from 1311 to 1548

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the pyramid to have been overtaken by a skyscraper or a modern tower; realising it was medieval England narrows it to the only thing medieval Europe built that tall, which is a satisfying 'of course' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Lincoln Cathedral (a cathedral) is widely credited with surpassing the Great Pyramid c.1311 and held the record until 1548; the spire height is doubted by some but the claim is standard.

explanation: The central spire of Lincoln Cathedral is thought to have passed the pyramid's height around 1311, and no building in the world rivalled the pyramid before that.

question: Japan's Akashi Kaikyō Bridge, the longest suspension span in the world when it opened in 1998, ended up about one metre longer than its blueprints. What stretched it while it was still being built?
source_excerpt: the central span had to be increased by 1 m (3.3 ft).

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a bridge ends up longer because engineers changed the plans; the idea that the ground itself moved the finished towers apart is a shock, yet 'Japan' plus 'stretched' gives a thinking player a real route to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: The 1995 Kobe earthquake moved the towers during construction, adding 1 m to the central span; the 2022 Çanakkale record doesn't affect the past-tense 'when it opened' claim (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akashi_Kaikyō_Bridge).

explanation: The 1995 Kobe earthquake shifted the already-built towers apart, so the engineers simply adjusted the design to the new, slightly longer span.

question: Opened in 2004 and designed with architect Norman Foster, which cable-stayed motorway bridge in southern France rises higher at its tallest point than the Eiffel Tower?
source_excerpt: 13 m taller than the 330-metre Eiffel Tower

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the Eiffel Tower is the tallest structure France has ever built; the overturn is that a motorway bridge in a rural valley quietly tops it, and the Norman Foster and 2004 footholds give a motivated player a real route to the name.
extra.verification_notes: Millau Viaduct opened Dec 2004, Foster-designed, cable-stayed, 343 m pylon vs Eiffel Tower 330 m; losing the world's-tallest-bridge title in 2025 doesn't affect the question's claims (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millau_Viaduct).

explanation: Its tallest mast reaches about 343 metres above the base, a little over the roughly 330 metres of the Eiffel Tower, as it carries the A75 motorway across the Tarn valley.
